title: A Quantum Coherence Microscope in the Hubbard Regime
authors: Lin Su, Michal Szurek, Alec Douglas, Ceren B. Dag, Markus Greiner
abstract: Quantum coherence underlies collective quantum phenomena and emerging quantum technologies. Quantum gas microscopes have transformed quantum simulation by providing projective snapshots of many-body states with single-atom resolution, but spatially resolved measurements of off-diagonal correlations have remained elusive. Here, using the Talbot effect, we introduce a quantum coherence microscope that maps off-diagonal correlations onto site-resolved density signals with near-single-site resolution. We use this technique to locally probe the superfluid-Mott transition in a layer of a three-dimensional optical lattice and to measure coherence beyond nearest neighbors in an engineered potential landscape. By mapping off-diagonal correlations onto density signals through controlled Talbot evolution, this work opens new possibilities for accessing observables beyond the density basis through tailored matter-wave evolution and recapture.
summary: The paper presents a novel 'quantum coherence microscope' using the Talbot effect applied to ultracold atoms in optical lattices. This technique maps hard-to-measure off-diagonal quantum correlations onto measurable site-resolved density modulations. It successfully applies this method to characterize fundamental physics, such as mapping out the superfluid-Mott transition locally and measuring long-range coherence.
main_problem: The primary challenge is achieving spatially resolved measurements of off-diagonal quantum correlations (coherence) beyond simple local density measurements in interacting many-body systems.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated a technique to map these elusive off-diagonal coherence signals onto measurable site-resolved density modulations, enabling the local probing of phase transitions like the superfluid-Mott transition.
method: They introduce a 'quantum coherence microscope' that utilizes controlled time evolution (Talbot effect) followed by a phase-tunable recapture process to convert coherence information into density contrast signals.
model_or_system: The experiment uses ultracold atoms trapped in a three-dimensional optical lattice, simulating the Bose-Hubbard model. The system is studied across various regimes, including near the superfluid-Mott transition and on engineered ladder geometries.
key_observables: Normalized single-particle density matrix elements ($g^{(1)}_{i,j}$), which encode coherence; measured relative modulation amplitude ($R$) of the recapture filling.
important_parameters: Interaction strength to tunneling ratio ($U/t$), interchain tunneling ($t_\perp$), and lattice separation ($r$).
main_assumptions: The measurement relies on assuming that the relative modulation amplitude $R$ is independent of various system parameters (separation, filling, time) within the explored regime.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the technique using Talbot evolution to show revival patterns corresponding to different coherence ranges. Figure 2 demonstrates spatially resolving the SF-MI transition by measuring the recapture modulation in central versus edge regions. Figure 3 probes coherence on a ladder geometry as a function of interchain tunneling.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the fundamental limitation (measuring off-diagonal correlations), details the novel Talbot-based measurement technique, and then applies this method to study specific physical phenomena like the SF-MI transition in trapped systems and correlation decay on engineered lattices.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, non-destructive experimental tool for accessing higher-order quantum correlations that are typically difficult to measure directly, bridging the gap between density measurements and full coherence mapping in cold atom simulators.

Time-evolution simulation results are shown here assuming a lattice depth of 25 recoil energies. Panels a and b assume all sites have the same phase, whereas panels c and d show one realization of independent random phases uniformly distributed across the lattice sites. Panel e shows horizontal cuts through panels a and c at times t = 0 and t = TT/2 = 29µs. Panel f shows horizontal cuts of a and c at times t = 0 and t = TT = 58µs.
